import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 307

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/307](https://www.erdosproblems.com/307)
-/

namespace Erdos307

open scoped Finset

/--
Are there two finite set of primes $P$ and $Q$ such that

$$
1 = \left( \sum_{p \in P} \frac{1}{p} \right) \left( \sum_{q \in Q} \frac{1}{q} \right)
$$
?

Asked by Barbeau [Ba76].

[Ba76] Barbeau, E. J., _Computer challenge corner: Problem 477: A brute force program._
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_307 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ P Q : Finset ℕ, (∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime) ∧ (∀ q ∈ Q, q.Prime) ∧
    1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)⁻¹) * (∑ q ∈ Q, (q : ℚ)⁻¹) := by
  sorry

/--
Instead of asking for sets of primes, ask only that all elements in the sets be relatively coprime.

Cambie has found several examples when this weakened version is true. For example,
$$
1=\left(1+\frac{1}{5}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}\right)
$$
and
$$
1=\left(1+\frac{1}{41}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{7}\right).
$$
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_307.variants.coprime : answer(True) ↔ ∃ P Q : Finset ℕ, 0 ∉ P ∩ Q ∧ 1 < #P ∧ 1 < #Q ∧
    Set.Pairwise P Nat.Coprime ∧ Set.Pairwise Q Nat.Coprime ∧
    1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)⁻¹) * (∑ q ∈ Q, (q : ℚ)⁻¹) := by
  show True ↔ _
  simp only [Finset.mem_inter, not_and, true_iff]
  use {1, 5}, {2, 3}
  norm_num +decide

/--
There are no examples known of the weakened coprime version if we insist that $1\not\in P\cup Q$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_307.variants.coprime_one_notMem : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ P Q : Finset ℕ, 0 ∉ P ∩ Q ∧ 1 ∉ P ∪ Q ∧
    1 < #P ∧ 1 < #Q ∧ Set.Pairwise P Nat.Coprime ∧ Set.Pairwise Q Nat.Coprime ∧
    1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)⁻¹) * (∑ q ∈ Q, (q : ℚ)⁻¹) := by
  sorry

/--
A machine-checked **barrier** for Erdős 307 (Bonfioli, 2026): any solution with `Q` nonempty uses at
least 59 primes in total, and `(∏_{p ∈ P} p)² ≥ 4·10¹¹²` — i.e. `∏_{p ∈ P} p ≥ 2·10⁵⁶` (and, by
symmetry, the same for `∏ Q`); so no solution lies below a prime-product of `2.09·10⁵⁶`. The full
`sorry`-free proof is in the linked repository (`Closed.lean`): the left conjunct is `card_ge_59`,
the right is `erdos307_barrier_closed`. Both depend on `propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound` and
nothing further: the evaluation of the first 59 primes is kernel-checked by `decide`, so no
`native_decide` enters this statement.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
"https://github.com/ElVec1o/erdos307/blob/76d242b024102f32d8411c714be4ad140a8b7c4b/lean/Erdos307/Closed.lean#L121"]
theorem erdos_307.barrier {P Q : Finset ℕ}
    (hP : ∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime) (hQ : ∀ q ∈ Q, q.Prime) (hQne : Q.Nonempty)
    (heq : 1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)⁻¹) * (∑ q ∈ Q, (q : ℚ)⁻¹)) :
    59 ≤ #(P ∪ Q) ∧ (4 * 10 ^ 112 : ℚ) ≤ (∏ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)) ^ 2 := by
  sorry

end Erdos307

findings.description: The docstring's final numerical inference (line 79), “so no solution lies below a prime-product of 2.09·10⁵⁶”, overstates the bound in this declaration. The Lean conclusion is (∏ P)² ≥ 4·10¹¹², equivalent to ∏ P ≥ 2·10⁵⁶, not 2.09·10⁵⁶. The theorem and its formal_proof link are correct; the discrepancy is confined to the documentation.
findings.source_evidence: The cited Closed.lean explicitly distinguishes the two constants: “The paper's thm:barrier states the sharp 2.09·10⁵⁶; what is machine-checked here is the rounded 2·10⁵⁶ ... The sharp value is a paper result, not a Lean one.” See https://github.com/ElVec1o/erdos307/blob/76d242b024102f32d8411c714be4ad140a8b7c4b/lean/Erdos307/Closed.lean, introductory note and erdos307_barrier_closed.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the final docstring constant from 2.09·10⁵⁶ to 2·10⁵⁶, or explicitly describe 2.09·10⁵⁶ as a separate, sharper paper result rather than a consequence of this formal statement. No theorem change is needed.

reformulations.difference: Lean uses natural-number finsets, excludes zero only from P ∩ Q, and explicitly requires both cardinalities to exceed one. The source describes positive reciprocal denominators and does not explicitly impose those cardinality bounds.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The intersection condition does not permit any zero-denominator witness. A pairwise-coprime finset containing zero and having cardinality greater than one must be {0,1}. The other set is then zero-free, and the product equation forces its reciprocal sum to equal 1. A sum of unit fractions with positive pairwise-coprime denominators can be an integer only if every denominator is 1, contradicting that set's cardinality bound. Thus zero is absent from the union. The additional nontriviality requirements also leave the existential question unchanged: the source's witness P={1,5}, Q={2,3} satisfies them. Both the pointwise positivity equivalence and the full source existential equivalence were proved in /workspace/review/coprime.lean.

reformulations.difference: Lean includes 0 ∉ P ∩ Q and cardinality bounds, rather than simply asking for positive, pairwise-coprime denominators with 1 absent from both sets.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: With 1 excluded, pairwise coprimality and cardinality greater than one already exclude zero: zero can only be coprime to 1. Conversely, the source conditions force both cardinality bounds. An empty set makes the product zero; a singleton {n} would force the other reciprocal sum to equal the integer n. The integrality fact for pairwise-coprime positive denominators would then force its members to be 1, contradicting the source restriction and nonemptiness. A full pointwise equivalence to the positive, 1-free formulation without cardinality bounds was proved as ReviewCoprime.coprime_one_source_equivalence.
